sources.entry: 2. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) in Gitlab

summary.title: Dynamic application security testing (GitLab DAST)
summary.one_liner: GitLab's DAST documentation explains how runtime penetration testing of running web apps and APIs works, how analyzers run in CI/CD, and where scan results appear.
takeaways: DAST tests running web applications and APIs from the outside in, so it is language-neutral.
Use the DAST analyzer for web apps (including single page apps) and the API security analyzer for GraphQL, REST, and SOAP APIs.
Analyzers are configured through a CI/CD template and run scans in a Docker container, producing a DAST report artifact.
Results appear in merge requests, the pipeline security tab, and the vulnerability report; if any pipeline job fails, DAST output may not show.
The proxy-based DAST analyzer was deprecated in GitLab 16.9 and removed in 17.3; migration guides exist for proxy-based and browser-based analyzers.
summary.summary: The page is GitLab's reference for dynamic application security testing (DAST), which runs automated penetration-style tests against running web applications and APIs to find issues such as XSS, SQL injection, and CSRF. It describes the two analyzer types (DAST for web apps, API security for GraphQL, REST, and SOAP), how they run as CI/CD jobs in Docker containers, and how scan results are compared between source and target branches. It also covers where results appear and how to view the list of scanned URLs. The page notes the Ultimate tier requirement and migration notices for deprecated analyzers.
